title: Sharknado Probability Risk Analysis
text:
This report estimates the probability of a “sharknado” by incorporating real-world constraints and combining the probabilities of the events required for such an occurrence. Using available tornado data and reasonable assumptions, the analysis evaluates the likelihood of three key components:

The presence of a shark on the coast
A tornado moving coastal to inland
A tornado is strong enough to lift and move a shark inland

The analysis sequences the relevant probabilities to estimate the overall likelihood. A key assumption is that sharks are always present when a coastal-to-inland tornado occurs, which intentionally overestimates the probability and provides a conservative upper bound. The results indicate that, even under favorable assumptions, the probability of a sharknado is effectively zero. Only one tornado since 1950 shows the possibility of being a sharknado, an EF4 tornado from Florida in 1966.















Important



The probability of a sharknado is effectively zero. As such, no adjustments to insurance products are warranted. Resources should instead focus on higher-probability catastrophic events such as hurricanes and standard tornadoes.

title: 2  Introduction
text:
Extreme weather events have long piqued public and scientific interest, especially when their consequences can be extremely dangerous for human life. Among these, the concept of a “sharknado,” a tornado capable of lifting sharks from the ocean and throwing them inland, represents an exaggerated but intriguing scenario. While such an event is widely seen as fictional, evaluating a sharknado’s plausibility provides an opportunity to apply probabilistic reasoning within real-world constraints.
This project aims to estimate the probability of a sharknado occurring by breaking up the phenomenon into a sequence of events that need to occur. In the methods section, we outline the sequence of these probabilities. These include the probability of a tornado forming near a coastal region and moving inward, the probability that such a tornado reaches a sufficient intensity to pick up and move a shark, and the assumption that a shark is present at the exact location required. To ensure a conservative upper estimate for this probability, several assumptions are intentionally biased in favor of the event occurring, such as a constant availability of sharks along coastlines and the ability for high magnitude earthquakes to pick them up and transport them inland.

    A(Tornado forms near coast) --> B(Tornado moves inland)
    B --> C(Tornado strong enough to lift shark)
    C --> D(Shark present at location)
    D --> E((SHARKNADO))








Figure 2.1: Flowchart illustrating the sequence of events leading to a Sharknado.



Using a combination of probabilistic reasoning and simplifying assumptions, the analysis synthesizes these individual components into an overall estimate for the probability of the occurrence of a sharknado. These results provide insight not only into the probability of a sharknado, but also into how compounding rare events together quickly diminishes the overall probability.

In the original US tornado data set from the NOAA, many tornadoes have missing ending latitudes and longitudes, specifically they were marked as “0” instead of “NA”. This can’t be right however since the 0 latitude line and the 0 longitude line do not intersect North America anywhere. Figure 3.1 below shows the 0 latitude and 0 longitude lines.
As such, these tornadoes in the data set are taken to be rows with missing values. The total percentage of missing end coordinates relative to the entire data set is \(\frac{24009}{68747}\) ≈ 34.92%. It should be examined whether these tornadoes have some sort of trend relative to the other tornadoes in the data set, so that it can be determined if they can be removed without worry. Specifically, there are two possible concerns: whether tornadoes in a certain area have a significantly higher chance of missing end values, and whether tornadoes of different magnitudes are more likely to have missing end coordinates than others. To examine the first concern, two figures can be created. Figure 3.2 shows the location of all tornadoes in the data set, and Figure 3.3 shows the location of only the tornadoes that have a missing value for the ending latitude or longitude.
Figure 3.2: Starting locations of all tornadoes in the continental United States.
Figure 3.3: Starting locations of tornadoes with missing end coordinates.
There is no apparent trend in the missing end coordinates. Their geographic distribution is similar to that of all tornadoes, suggesting that the first concern is alleviated.
To address the second concern regarding magnitude, we create plots for each magnitude level (see Figure 3.4 and Figure 3.5) to examine whether the rate of missing end coordinates varies by magnitude compared to the overall pattern in the full dataset.
Figure 3.4: Starting locations of all tornadoes in the continental United States grouped by magnitude on EF scale
Figure 3.5: Starting locations of tornadoes with missing end coordinates grouped by magnitude on EF scale
From these plots, it appears that higher magnitude tornadoes occur more frequently in the Midwest and South and less often on the West Coast. However, this pattern is consistent with the plots of all tornadoes separated by magnitude. Therefore, while there is some variation by magnitude, excluding tornadoes with missing end coordinates should not heavily bias the analysis, as the trends in magnitude are similar between the full data set and the subset with missing end coordinates.

title: 4  Results
text:
Now, we need to compute the probabilities for each tornado type that we have classified. This can be done quite simply by dividing the number of tornadoes that we have classified to each tornado type by the total number of tornadoes. The results are summarized in the following table:

As shown, there are far fewer coastal-to-inland tornadoes compared with inland-to-coastal and other tornadoes. This relatively small amount reflects the strict requirement that the tornado must start within a short distance of the coast to be classified in this category.
Lastly, we estimate the probability that a tornado is strong enough to lift a shark, conditional on it being coastal-to-inland. According to NOAA Fisheries (2025), great white sharks can weigh up to 4,500 lbs. Similarly, Quach (2025) reports that the average car weighs approximately 4,419 lbs, suggesting that great white sharks are of comparable mass to cars. From Otero Property Adjusting & Appraisals (2025), EF3 tornadoes are “likely to toss cars and trucks,” whereas EF4 tornadoes are “very likely to toss cars many feet.” This indicates that at least an EF4 tornado would be required, since a sharknado would require sharks not only to be lifted, but also transported a substantial distance inland rather than merely displaced. These sharks must be pulled out of the water as well, which adds to the wind speed necessary. This gives all the more reason to rule out EF3 tornadoes and only consider EF4 and EF5. To compute this probability, we first have to define the number of tornadoes for each combination of magnitude \(m\) and movement type \(t\), call this \(N_{m,t}\). The probability of a tornado having magnitude \(m\) given movement type \(t\) is the number of tornadoes with magnitude \(m\) and movement type \(t\) divided by the total number of tornadoes with movement type \(t\).
\[
P(\text{Magnitude} = m|\text{Movement} = t) = \frac{N_{m,t}}{\sum_{m} N_{m,t}}
\] For our specific probability we are interested in this probability where m = 4 or 5, and t = coastal to inland.
Computing this probability we get:
\[
\frac{1 + 0}{417}
\approx 0.24\%
\quad
(1 \text{ from magnitude 4},\ 0 \text{ from magnitude 5})
\] The one tornado that we have seen to satisfy our conditions for a sharknado occurred on April 4, 1966. The location where it first touched down is below:









While this one tornado satisfies the defined conditions, it relies on strong assumptions. A shark would need to be present along the coastline at the moment of formation, and EF4 winds would truly need to be capable of lifting it from the water. If either assumption fails, this case is excluded, leaving a 0% probability of sharknados in the observed data.

title: 5  Conclusion
text:
The analysis demonstrates that even under highly favorable assumptions, the probability of a sharknado occurring remains extremely low. By breaking down the event into a series of necessary events, each with a very small likelihood, the combined probability becomes effectively zero. Notably, the assumption that sharks are always available along the coastline and that tornadoes of sufficient magnitude can lift them inland represents a significant overestimation, reinforcing that the calculated probability serves as a conservative upper estimate, rather than a realistic expectation.
This extremely low probability is to be expected as we are forcing many rare events to occur simultaneously. When this happens, the overall probability decreases dramatically. This idea extends beyond the concept of sharknadoes and is relevant for other concerns where many rare events need to occur together. In these scenarios, the overall likelihood will drop dramatically as the sharknado probability did.
Future work could build upon this analysis by incorporating more realistic environmental constraints, such as the distribution of shark locations and the physics-based modeling of lifting forces required for moving sharks. Ultimately, while sharnadoes are far from realistic, the analytical approach used in this study shows the power of probabilistic reasoning in exploring even the most unusual problems.

text:
3.2 Probability Layout
To examine the potential risk of a sharknado, we compute the probability of such an event occurring. From the perspective of any tornado occurring in the United States, this probability can be expressed as the product of several individual probabilities: \[
P(\text{sharknado}) =
P(\text{shark is present}) \times
P(\text{tornado is coastal to inland}) \times
P(\text{tornado is strong enough to lift a shark})
\] Alternatively, if we focus specifically on tornadoes that are coastal-to-inland, the probability of a sharknado occurring conditional on this event can be written as:
\[
P(\text{sharknado | tornado is coastal to inland}) =
P(\text{shark is present}) \times
P(\text{tornado is strong enough to lift a shark | tornado is coastal to inland})
\]
The latter case is likely the better answer to our question, as we are worried about the possibility of sharknados occurring when there is a coastal to inland tornado, not when there is a tornado anywhere. As such, the following analysis will focus on this conditional framework.
To obtain a conservative upper bound on this probability, we assume that \(P(\text{shark is present}) = 1\). In other words, we assume that whenever a coastal-to-inland tornado occurs, a shark is present near the coast and available to be lifted. While this assumption is unrealistic, it provides an upper bound on the probability of a sharknado. This strengthens the conclusion if the resulting probability remains small.
To begin, we classify each tornado as coastal-to-inland, inland-to-coastal, or neither. While this could be simplified to a binary classification (coastal-to-inland versus not coastal-to-inland), we include the inland-to-coastal category for completeness and to allow comparison between movement directions.
The classification threshold for “coastal-to-inland” tornadoes requires that the tornado’s starting location be within 10,000 meters of the nearest coast and that its ending location be farther from the coast than its starting location. Similarly, tornadoes are classified as “inland-to-coastal” if their starting location is more than 10,000 meters from the nearest coast and their ending location is closer to the coast than their starting location.

3.2 Probability And Classification Layout
To examine the potential risk of a sharknado, we compute the probability of such an event occurring. From the perspective of any tornado occurring in the United States, this probability can be expressed as the product of several individual probabilities:
\[
\begin{gathered}
P(\text{sharknado}) = P(\text{shark is present}) \times \\
P(\text{tornado is coastal to inland}) \times
P(\text{tornado is strong enough to lift a shark})
\end{gathered}
\]
Alternatively, if we focus specifically on tornadoes that are coastal-to-inland, the probability of a sharknado occurring conditional on this event can be written as:
\[
\begin{gathered}
P(\text{sharknado} \mid \text{tornado is coastal to inland}) = P(\text{shark is present}) \times \\
P(\text{tornado is strong enough to lift a shark} \mid \text{tornado is coastal to inland})
\end{gathered}
\]
The latter case is likely the better answer to our question, as we are worried about the possibility of sharknados occurring when there is a coastal to inland tornado, not when there is a tornado anywhere. As such, the following analysis will focus on this conditional framework.
To obtain a conservative upper bound on this probability, we assume that \(P(\text{shark is present}) = 1\). In other words, we assume that whenever a coastal-to-inland tornado occurs, a shark is present near the coast and available to be lifted. While this assumption is unrealistic, it provides an upper bound on the probability of a sharknado. This strengthens the conclusion if the resulting probability remains small.

While this could be simplified to a binary classification (coastal-to-inland versus not coastal-to-inland), we include the inland-to-coastal category for completeness and to allow comparison between movement directions.
The classification threshold for “coastal-to-inland” tornadoes requires that the tornado’s starting location be within 10,000 meters of the nearest coast and that its ending location be farther from the coast than its starting location. Similarly, tornadoes are classified as “inland-to-coastal” if their starting location is more than 10,000 meters from the nearest coast and their ending location is closer to the coast than their starting location.
